props.title: The Hills Run Red

sections.content: The Hills Run Red (2009) stands as a meta-horror masterpiece that deconstructs our obsession with lost exploitation films. Like Behind the Mask: The Rise of Leslie Vernon (2006), it cleverly examines horror fandom while delivering genuine scares. The film follows film student Tyler, who becomes obsessed with tracking down a legendary lost slasher film called "The Hills Run Red" - only to discover its director Concannon has never stopped filming. It shares DNA with Peeping Tom (1960) in its exploration of the relationship between violence and filmmaking.

sections.content: The film's commentary on exploitation cinema recalls Grindhouse (2007) and Hobo with a Shotgun (2011), but pushes further into genuine darkness. Director Dave Parker crafts a sophisticated meditation on horror fandom that asks uncomfortable questions about why we're drawn to extreme cinema. The masked killer Babyface becomes an iconic slasher figure, joining the ranks of Leslie Vernon (2006) and The Collector (2009) as modern horror icons who comment on the genre itself.

Like 8MM (1999) and Videodrome (1983), The Hills Run Red explores the dangerous allure of underground film and how far people will go to capture authentic horror. The movie's structure cleverly mirrors classic slashers while subverting expectations, similar to how Cabin in the Woods (2011) plays with horror conventions. The film-within-a-film concept creates layers of meta-commentary that reward horror scholars while maintaining accessibility for casual viewers. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Meta-Horror

sections.content: The Hills Run Red represents a crucial evolution in self-aware horror, building on foundations laid by Wes Craven's New Nightmare (1994) and Man Bites Dog (1992). Its exploration of film preservation and lost media anxiety connects to films like Sinister (2012) and V/H/S (2012), while its commentary on exploitation filmmaking recalls Tesis (1996) and Effects (1980).
